So, C is used for embedded systems. The best way to describe this is: C runs on "bare metal." Chances are, you don't actually interact with C. It's low-level, and it's used on hardware.

Things like your IoT thermostat, your modem/router, and your phone is coded in C. You're not actually using the software/firmware running on your router, but rest assure there's code running on it to turn bits/bytes into a YouTube video on your computer.

C++ on the other hand is more "robust." Programs and games can be written in C++, as well as software you interact with (phone apps, computer games, etc.). C++ "encapsulates" C (anything you can do with C you can do with C++), but you wouldn't put C++ on an IoT coffee maker with limited memory and resources.

C++ is also object oriented, where C is not... but that's a little advanced, especially if you haven't coded before.

It all really boils down to what you want to do with your coding. Do you want to develop for hardware (Linux/OSx kernel, remote controls, microcontrollers, etc) -- if so, go for C. Do you want abstraction and high-level programs that can run any number of algorithms easily -- you're looking for C++. Do you want to develop web apps and games -- then you're probably looking at Ruby, on Rails JavaScript, PHP, and Apache. Are you looking for a quick intro, to get your feet wet, and understand syntax and how coding works (broad spectrum) -- go for a scripting language like Python.

If there is a particular software project that you use or want to work on then learn the language it uses. Since I am a C programmer I will say you should learn that because I hate much of C++ but I acknowledge that many people think C++ is better.

Which language (C or C++) will depend largely on what you intend to do with it. C is generally used for (but certainly not limited to) low level drivers and firmware. C++ is a different programming paradigm than C, object orientated or procedural, respectively. It is used in writing applications mostly.
